content: The data analyzed includes 5,765 participants from four randomized controlled trials. The absolute difference in outcomes was 19 fewer events per 1,000 participants, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 16 fewer to 4 fewer events per 1,000. The evidence quality was rated as high. The time to hospital discharge was assessed based on data from 113 participants in three randomized controlled trials. However, due to serious imprecision, the evidence quality was rated as moderate. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for malaria, updated on October 16, 2023, indicate that 427 out of 451 standard doses of artesunate and quinine (with loading doses) were used. In the artesunate group, eight events were reported. The imprecision was not considered serious, and the 95% CI of the pooled effect suggests a clinically significant benefit with artesunate. The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one childhood death was calculated as 38. However, there was a serious risk of bias, as 24% of patients with neurological sequelae at discharge were not available for assessment at day 28. The trial was conducted across 11 centers in Africa, using standard dosing of artesunate and quinine. The nature of the neurological sequelae was not described, but the imprecision was not serious, and the 95% CI around the absolute effect was narrow. There was a 2% increase in neurological sequelae at day 28, but the risk of bias was not serious. Allocation concealment was adequate, and the trials were considered to have a low risk of bias. Although the trials were unblinded, this was unlikely to have influenced the objective outcomes. There was no statistical heterogeneity between trials (I² = 0%), and the data were primarily derived from a single multicenter trial conducted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, Uganda, and Tanzania. The effect estimate for artesunate indicates clinically important harm, but the 95% CI includes the possibility of no clinically significant difference between artesunate and quinine. The trials adequately concealed allocation and were considered to have a low risk of bias. There was no statistical heterogeneity between trials (I² = 0%). The evidence was derived from multiple sites in Asia (Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam), and both trials used standard drug doses. The results were statistically significant in favor of artesunate, with adequate sample size to detect a 40% risk reduction with 80% power and 95% confidence. Neurological sequelae were rare after severe malaria in adults, but the 95% CI includes the possibility of clinically significant harm with artesunate. The large multicenter study adequately concealed allocation and was considered to have a low risk of bias, while the smaller trial did not. Neither trial was blinded. The data could not be pooled due to differences in reporting (medians, ranges, or interquartile ranges). There was no evidence of a clinically significant benefit with artesunate for this outcome. The coma resolution time was based on data from 494 participants in two randomized controlled trials. The data were not pooled due to serious imprecision, and the evidence quality was rated as moderate. Parasite clearance time was also assessed in the same two trials, with no pooling of data. The trials were generally well-conducted and had a low risk of bias. There was no statistical heterogeneity, and the studies were conducted in Thailand and Vietnam, comparing intramuscular artemether with intravenous artesunate in adults. However, the trials and meta-analysis lacked adequate power to detect a difference in mortality or to prove equivalence. The fever clearance time was based on data from 494 participants in two randomized controlled trials. The data were not pooled, and there was no evidence of a benefit with artesunate for this outcome. The trials were conducted in East and West Africa and India, primarily in children with severe malaria (aged <15 years), comparing intramuscular artemether with intravenous quinine. The meta-analysis had adequate power to detect a statistically significant effect, but the clinical importance of the result is uncertain. The mean difference in parasite clearance time ranged from a 2-hour increase with artemether to a 15-hour decrease. The meta-analysis had adequate power to detect a statistically significant effect, but the clinical importance of the result is uncertain. The coma resolution time was based on data from 683 participants in three randomized controlled trials. The data were not pooled due to serious inconsistency and imprecision. Parasite clearance time was based on data from 716 participants in four trials, with no pooling of data. The trials were conducted in Thailand, Papua New Guinea, and Vietnam, comparing intramuscular artemether with intravenous quinine in adults. The meta-analysis results were statistically significant, with low heterogeneity among trials.
